eyebrow: Python for Data Engineers · Chapter 4, Lesson 22
subtitle: Fixing orders.csv's two real problems — properly, with pandas.

code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
print(df.isna().sum())

# customer_name   1
# (every other column: 0)
caption: df.isna() returns a True/False grid; .sum() counts the True values per column — exactly one, on order 1005.

eyebrow: fillna(): a clear placeholder, not a guess
code:
df["customer_name"] = df["customer_name"].fillna("Unknown Customer")
print(df.loc[df["order_id"] == 1005, "customer_name"])

# 4    Unknown Customer
caption: Customer 504 appears on no other row, so there's nothing real to recover — dropna() would lose otherwise-good revenue data.

eyebrow: duplicated(): the obvious check is wrong here
code:
print(df.duplicated(subset=["customer_name"]).sum())
# 7  <- real customers who ordered more than once, NOT duplicates

print(df.duplicated(subset=["order_id"]).sum())
# 0  <- the subset that actually finds accidental duplicates
caption: duplicated() only tells you what you asked it to check. Checking by name would flag Dana Whitfield's real, separate orders.

code:
bad_qty = df["quantity"] < 0
df_clean = df[~bad_qty].copy()
print(len(df), "->", len(df_clean))

# 20 -> 19
caption: isna() won't catch a negative number — it needs its own check. ~bad_qty flips the mask: "keep everything NOT bad."
